entries.originalText: Those things which a man cannot amend in himself or in others, he ought patiently to bear, until God shall otherwise ordain.
entries.modernizedText: A person ought patiently to bear those things he cannot amend in himself or in others, until God ordains otherwise.

entries.originalText: Bethink thee that perhaps it is better for thy trial and patience, without which our merits are but little worth.
entries.modernizedText: Consider that perhaps it is better for your testing and patience, without which our merits are worth little.

entries.originalText: Nevertheless thou oughtest, when thou findeth such impediments, to beseech God that He would vouchsafe to sustain thee, that thou be able to bear them with a good will.
entries.modernizedText: Nevertheless, when you encounter such obstacles, you ought to ask God graciously to sustain you, so that you can bear them willingly.

entries.originalText: If one who is once or twice admonished refuse to hearken, strive not with him, but commit all to God, that His will may be done and His honour be shown in His servants, for He knoweth well how to convert the evil unto good.
entries.modernizedText: If someone who is admonished once or twice refuses to listen, do not strive with him, but commit everything to God, so that His will may be done and His honor shown in His servants, for He knows well how to turn evil into good.

entries.originalText: Endeavour to be patient in bearing with other men’s faults and infirmities whatsoever they be, for thou thyself also hast many things which have need to be borne with by others.
entries.modernizedText: Endeavor to be patient in bearing with other people’s faults and infirmities, whatever they may be, for you yourself also have many things that others need to bear with.

entries.originalText: If thou canst not make thine own self what thou desireth, how shalt thou be able to fashion another to thine own liking.
entries.modernizedText: If you cannot make yourself what you desire, how will you be able to shape another to your own liking?

entries.originalText: We are ready to see others made perfect, and yet we do not amend our own shortcomings.
entries.modernizedText: We are ready to see others made perfect, and yet we do not amend our own shortcomings.

entries.originalText: We will that others be straitly corrected, but we will not be corrected ourselves.
entries.modernizedText: We want others to be strictly corrected, but we will not be corrected ourselves.

entries.originalText: The freedom of others displeaseth us, but we are dissatisfied that our own wishes shall be denied us.
entries.modernizedText: The freedom of others displeases us, but we are dissatisfied when our own wishes are denied.

entries.originalText: We desire rules to be made restraining others, but by no means will we suffer ourselves to be restrained.
entries.modernizedText: We desire rules to be made to restrain others, but will by no means allow ourselves to be restrained.

entries.originalText: Thus therefore doth it plainly appear how seldom we weigh our neighbour in the same balance with ourselves.
entries.modernizedText: Thus it plainly appears how seldom we weigh our neighbor in the same balance as ourselves.

entries.originalText: If all men were perfect, what then should we have to suffer from others for God?
entries.modernizedText: If everyone were perfect, what then would we have to suffer from others for God?

entries.originalText: But now hath God thus ordained, that we may learn to bear one another’s burdens, because none is without defect, none without a burden, none sufficient of himself, none wise enough of himself; but it behoveth us to bear with one another, to comfort one another, to help, instruct, admonish one another.
entries.modernizedText: But God has now ordained it so that we may learn to bear one another’s burdens, because no one is without defect, no one without a burden, no one sufficient of himself, no one wise enough of himself; but we must bear with one another, comfort one another, and help, instruct, and admonish one another.

entries.originalText: How much strength each man hath is best proved by occasions of adversity: for such occasions do not make a man frail, but show of what temper he is.
entries.modernizedText: How much strength each person has is best proved by occasions of adversity, for such occasions do not make a person frail, but show what his character is.
